opus-5.5.text:
For me it came down to timing and where the real bottleneck was moving.

When large language models started to take off, most of the attention went to training: bigger models, more data, more GPUs. But I kept thinking that once these models are trained, the real cost and the real impact happen when people actually *use* them. Inference runs every time someone sends a request, millions or billions of times. So making inference fast, cheap, and easy to deploy seemed like one of the most important problems in the whole stack, and it was underserved compared to training.

vLLM had a very clear technical insight at its core. PagedAttention treated the KV cache the way an operating system treats memory, with paging instead of big contiguous chunks. That idea is simple to explain but has a huge practical effect on throughput. When I saw it, I felt this wasn't an incremental trick. It was the right abstraction, and good abstractions tend to become foundations other people build on.

The second reason was open source. I've always cared about building infrastructure that many people can use, not just one company. An open-source inference engine sits at a very interesting point. Model developers want their models to run well on it, hardware vendors want their chips supported, and users want one place where everything just works. If a project becomes that common layer, the leverage is enormous. Every improvement you make benefits the whole ecosystem at once.

And honestly, there was a personal fit too. My background is in machine learning systems and compilers, things like torch.compile, so I understood both the model side and the low-level performance side. vLLM needed exactly that combination. It felt like a place where my skills could have outsized impact.

So it was a mix: a problem that was clearly going to matter more and more, a strong technical foundation, an open community with real momentum, and a role where I could contribute something meaningful. When those line up, you don't get many chances like that, so I decided to go all in.

r001.rationale: The response cites inference’s importance, PagedAttention, open source, and personal fit, but does not say Kaichao expected vLLM to continue Berkeley’s lineage of projects.

fable-5.1.text:
When I first came across vLLM, I was still a PhD student at Tsinghua, and honestly my background was more on the research side of deep learning, not systems. But what struck me about vLLM was the timing and the nature of the problem.

Think about where things stood in 2023. Everyone was talking about large models, but the bottleneck for actually using them was inference. Training gets all the glory, but if you want a model to serve millions of people, inference cost and throughput decide whether the thing is viable at all. vLLM came out of Berkeley with PagedAttention, and that single idea, borrowing virtual memory concepts from operating systems to manage the KV cache, gave it a huge jump in throughput. That told me the project had real technical substance, not just hype.

The second thing was that it was open source and still very young. The codebase was small enough that one person could read through all of it and understand how it worked end to end. That's a rare window. In a mature project like PyTorch, contributing meaningfully takes years of context. In vLLM at that stage, if you understood CUDA, distributed execution, and PyTorch internals, you could make a real difference quickly. I had spent a lot of time digging into PyTorch, especially torch.compile and the distributed stack, so I felt I had something concrete to offer.

And the third thing is more personal. I've always believed infrastructure is where a lot of leverage sits. If you write a paper, maybe a few hundred people read it. If you fix a bug in the serving engine that a large share of the industry runs on, that improvement shows up everywhere, immediately. For someone who wants their work to matter, that is very attractive.

So I started by filing issues and small fixes, then gradually took on bigger pieces like the distributed communication layer and later the torch.compile integration. The community was welcoming, the maintainers were responsive, and every contribution got used almost right away. Once you experience that feedback loop, it's hard to go back. That's why I decided it was worth committing to seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says vLLM came out of Berkeley and describes its technical merits, but it does not identify an expectation that vLLM would continue Berkeley’s lineage of projects as a reason for committing.

astra-6.text:
For me, the attraction was the gap between having a powerful model and making it useful in practice. Inference is where people actually interact with the model, so improving that part of the system can have a very direct impact.

I saw vLLM as an opportunity to work on that gap. There are interesting technical problems, but there’s also a clear practical question: can we help people run their models more efficiently and make them easier to use? That combination of technical depth and practical value was what made it worth committing my energy to.

r001.rationale: The response says vLLM could help people run models efficiently and make them easier to use, but does not mention Berkeley or continuing its project lineage as a reason for committing.

sol-6.1.text:
What attracted me to vLLM was the chance to work on a practical bottleneck. A language model can be very capable, but making it fast and affordable enough for people to use is a whole other challenge. Inference is where those questions become concrete: how efficiently you use memory, how many requests you can serve, and how long people have to wait.

I saw an opportunity to bring systems work directly into that experience. A performance improvement can help many people running different models and building different applications. And with an open-source project, that work can compound: people contribute ideas, test them in different settings, and help make the system better. That combination of technical depth and practical impact made it feel worth committing my energy to.

r001.rationale: The response cites practical impact, systems work, and open-source collaboration as reasons for committing to vLLM, but does not mention continuing Berkeley’s project lineage.
